svg.aria-label: Diagram: the four landing zone design areas of identity provisioning, resource hierarchy, network and security controls, the options within each, and how the cost of changing each decision later drives the order they should be made in
svg.title: Landing zone design: four areas, several answers each, and wildly different costs to change your mind
svg.text: Modular means designed separately. It does not mean equally reversible.
Four areas to decide. Order them by how hard each is to undo, not by how satisfying each is to discuss.
1. Identity provisioning — decide first
Google as the primary source, no federation.
Federate an existing IdP — AD, Entra ID, Okta.
Workforce Identity Federation, no Cloud Identity.
Highest cost to change: it is a contract with the
rest of the company, and the one area the cloud
team does not own.
2. Network design — four options, not two
Shared VPC per environment — the default.
Hub-and-spoke with appliances — L7 inspection.
Hub-and-spoke without — shared on-prem, autonomy.
Private Service Connect — teams keep their own IPs.
High cost: workloads come to depend on the paths,
so changing topology means changing workloads.
3. Resource hierarchy
Folders, projects, and where policy attaches.
Moderate cost: projects can move between folders,
but policy inheritance moves with them.
Inventory what exists before designing this.
4. Security controls — seven of them
Limit persistent credentials for service accounts.
Mitigate data exfiltration through Google APIs.
Centrally aggregate necessary logs. Plus monitoring,
encryption at rest and in transit, provider access.
Lowest cost to change — mostly org policy.
The caveat on “controls are cheap to change”
They are cheap to change and expensive to APPLY LATE, which is a different claim. Post #22: enforcement is not
retroactive, so the same policy set in year three is a remediation project per constraint.
So decide the controls last if you must — but apply them first. The decision and the deployment can be separated.
Which inverts the usual order of work
Security controls are easiest to talk about, produce the most satisfying checklist, and are cheapest to defer.
Identity is least interesting to a cloud team and most expensive to get wrong.
A programme that opens with a controls workshop and leaves federation “with the identity team” is backwards.
What the blueprint in #29 assumes that a real organisation may not have
No existing identity provider · a team that owns the address space · an empty organisation to build a
hierarchy in · one set of requirements. The Private Service Connect design exists because the second is
sometimes false, and more than one landing zone exists because the fourth often is.
A simple test for whether a landing zone effort is ordered sensibly:
ask which decisions have actually been made, and check them against how hard each is to undo. Three months in
with a controls matrix and no federation answer means the irreversible work will be settled by whatever ships first.
